name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Friday 14 September 1973

clue.text: Such a clue's ideal for a letter-sorter

definitions.text: Such a clue's ideal for a letter-sorter

blocks.note: surface reading: a post-office worker sorting the mail

blocks.clueFragment: Such a clue's ideal for a letter-sorter
blocks.note: setter's reading: someone who rearranges letters into words likes a clue built on scrambled letters

explanation.walkthrough: The post office is the false scene; the letters being sorted are the alphabet's, and the clue type that rewards rearranging them is the one named.
explanation.definitionFit: An anagram clue is solved by reordering letters, so it suits anyone whose pastime is shuffling them into new words.

clue.text: Play part, over a long time, of one hounded to death

indicators.note: in a down entry one thing over another sits above it, so the first piece is written before the second

blocks.note: to act is to play a part
an aeon is an immensely long period

explanation.surface: An actor has spent ages playing a persecuted character.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the hunter Actaeon saw Artemis bathing, was turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical hunter was literally killed by his own hunting dogs, so the phrase describes him exactly.

clue.text: Concede it has a little mark on it

indicators.note: in a down entry something on another is placed above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: taken as written
DM, the short form of the Deutschmark
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone owns up that the thing has a small blemish on it.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'little mark' is the abbreviation of the German currency, the Deutschmark, not a smudge.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit something is to acknowledge or grant that it is true, which is to concede it.

clue.text: More heavenly joy from this baddie than from 99 goodies

definitions.text: More heavenly joy from this baddie than from 99 goodies

blocks.note: surface reading: a villain who somehow earns more praise than many good people

blocks.clueFragment: More heavenly joy from this baddie than from 99 goodies
blocks.note: setter's reading: Luke 15:7, joy in heaven over one sinner who turns from sin, more than over ninety-nine just persons

explanation.walkthrough: The clue paraphrases the parable of the lost sheep, where heaven rejoices most over the one sinner who changes his ways.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospel's sinner who earns heaven's joy is one who is sorry for his sins and turns from them.

clue.text: Average-sounding air

indicators.note: something sounding like a word is heard rather than read, so the spelling changes but the pronunciation stays

blocks.note: the mean is the arithmetic average

explanation.surface: A tune or atmosphere that is only middling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' looks like a tune or the atmosphere but means bearing; the homophone is spelt the old way with an I.
explanation.definitionFit: An air is a person's manner or appearance, which is what a mien is.

clue.text: Statesman

blocks.note: surface reading: a senior politician
setter's reading: split into States-man, a man from the States

explanation.walkthrough: The single word reads as a politician; split, it describes a native of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the United States, known simply as the States, is a citizen of that country.

clue.text: The fashionable crowd does not take up the whole page

definitions.text: does not take up the whole page
definitions.note: a description of the answer rather than a synonym

blocks.note: what is in is in fashion
a set is a social group or clique

explanation.surface: The smart social crowd will not fill a whole magazine page.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a small picture or map placed within a larger page, so it fills only part of it.

clue.text: Bellman hunted with him

blocks.note: surface reading: the Bellman who leads the hunt in Lewis Carroll's The Hunting of the Snark
setter's reading: Bellman is a hound named in the hunting song 'D'ye ken ...', alongside Ranter, Ringwood and True

explanation.walkthrough: The Snark hunt is the false trail. The famous English hunting song lists the huntsman's hounds, and Bellman is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cumbrian huntsman of the folk song rode out with his pack of hounds, one of which was named Bellman.

clue.text: Superior quarter — on which we may find beggars

definitions.text: on which we may find beggars

blocks.note: upper means higher in rank
south, one of the four compass quarters

explanation.surface: The posh district of a city is where you would find people begging.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'on one's uppers', the tops of shoes with the soles worn through, is an idiom for being penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'on one's uppers' means destitute, so beggars are found on them.

clue.text: Quarter of an hour for instance by this

definitions.text: Quarter of an hour for instance by this

blocks.note: surface reading: a stretch of fifteen minutes measured out

blocks.clueFragment: Quarter of an hour for instance by this
blocks.note: setter's reading: the instrument by which you tell that a quarter of an hour has passed

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a fragment of a timetable; 'by this' asks what device tells you the quarter hour.
explanation.definitionFit: A timepiece is any clock or watch, the instrument people read to know the time of day.

clue.text: In the Cheshire Cheese perhaps, it's exclusive in Fleet Street

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for a glass of beer, as drunk in a pub
second meaning: a story one newspaper gets before its rivals

explanation.walkthrough: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is a famous old pub on Fleet Street, the London street that stood for the British newspaper industry.
explanation.definitionFit: Pub slang calls a beer a scoop, and in journalism the word names an exclusive story beaten out of rival papers.

clue.text: The Mousetrap's story "—, and writ in very choice Italian"

definitions.text: The Mousetrap's story "—, and writ in very choice Italian"

blocks.note: surface reading: the plot of Agatha Christie's long-running London play

blocks.clueFragment: "—, and writ in very choice Italian"
blocks.note: setter's reading: Hamlet's line about his play-within-a-play, missing its one word

explanation.walkthrough: Christie's play is the false trail. Hamlet names the play he stages 'The Mousetrap' and says its tale 'is extant, and writ in very choice Italian'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means still in existence, as a surviving written story is.

clue.text: Length of a ball, including its break

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it apart, so the letters it acts on are set out in a new order
one thing including another holds it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a ball is a formal dance
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket coach measures how far a bowled ball travels, counting the spin it takes off the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows a stray '&' before 'a ball'; the wordplay reads without it. 'Ball' and 'break' feel like cricket, but the ball is a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Distance and length are synonyms for how far it is from one point to another.

clue.text: 36.9 degrees centigrade is not unusual

blocks.note: first meaning: the healthy human body temperature
second meaning: ordinary, standard

explanation.walkthrough: A thermometer reading this figure is what a doctor calls the standard body temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: A healthy temperature is described as normal, and normal also means ordinary or usual.

clue.text: Fashion houses make no bones about the Steptoe business

definitions.note: collective: the clothing industry as a whole

indicators.note: the idiom read literally says to leave the bones out, so that part of the phrase is dropped

blocks.note: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about rag-and-bone men, dealers in old junk

explanation.surface: Couturiers speak frankly about the junk-dealing trade.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip the bones (with their linking 'and') out of the rag-and-bone trade and the clothing industry's nickname remains.
explanation.definitionFit: The rag trade is a colloquial name for the clothing and fashion industry.

clue.text: Saint consumes a quarter of bread that's sweet?

indicators.note: whatever consumes something takes it inside, so one piece is swallowed by the other

blocks.note: St Pancras, early Roman martyr, known for the London church and station
east, one of the four compass quarters

explanation.surface: A holy man tucks into a chunk of loaf that turns out to be a sweet one.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: sweetbread is no bread and not sweet, but the cook's name for an animal's pancreas or thymus.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetbread is the culinary term for the pancreas (or thymus) of a calf or lamb served as offal.

clue.text: Far from dim over the bar

definitions.text: Far from dim over the bar

blocks.clueFragment: Far from dim over the bar
blocks.note: surface reading: someone quite bright, or a pub drinker who is no fool
setter's reading: dim. is the score abbreviation for diminuendo, and its opposite marked over a bar of music grows louder

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' and 'bar' suggest a pub or intelligence; in a musical score 'dim.' means get softer.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical instruction for growing louder is the opposite of diminuendo, and it is written over the bars it spans.

clue.text: Cock Robin death report — such pathos!

definitions.text: Cock Robin death report — such pathos!

blocks.note: surface reading: the nursery rhyme 'Who killed Cock Robin?'
setter's reading: in the rhyme all the birds of the air fell a-sighing and a-sobbing, which is the mawkish material asked for

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme's ending, with the birds 'a-sighing and a-sobbing', is the kind of tear-jerking stuff the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: Sentimental writing designed to make readers weep is called by this informal term for cheap pathos.

clue.text: Devils, self-styled, round at diplomat's house

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: the devils Jesus casts out in Mark's gospel say 'My name is Legion: for we are many'
taken as written

explanation.surface: Demons are said to be lurking around an embassy.
explanation.definitionFit: A legation is a diplomatic mission headed by a minister, and the building that houses it.

clue.text: Chairman's pet

blocks.note: surface reading: the favourite of a company chairman
setter's reading: a man in a chair has a lap, where a small pet dog sits

explanation.walkthrough: A seated man has a lap; the answer is also a sycophant who fawns on a boss, so both readings land.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pet dog kept on the lap, and by extension a servile follower who obeys a powerful person.

clue.text: Tom was crazy to go there

definitions.text: Tom was crazy to go there

blocks.clueFragment: Tom was crazy to go there
blocks.note: surface reading: someone called Tom took a foolish trip somewhere
setter's reading: Poor Tom, the traditional mad beggar of ballad and King Lear, named after the London asylum he came from

explanation.walkthrough: Edgar in King Lear disguises himself as 'Poor Tom', a madman of this kind; the place was the Bethlem Royal Hospital, London's asylum.
explanation.definitionFit: The old London madhouse gave its name to the word, so a crazy person was committed there.

clue.text: One in charge is perhaps a German

indicators.note: perhaps signals the phrase is only a possible version of the letters, so they may be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The boss might well be from Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: A manager is the person who runs or supervises a business or team.

clue.text: He takes off from Port Said, sort of

indicators.note: a sort of something is a loose version of it, so the letters are only roughly as given

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pilot is leaving the Egyptian harbour city on the Suez Canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes off' sounds like an aircraft leaving a port, but here it means mimics.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is to mimic them, which is what a parodist does for comic effect.

clue.text: His artful signature suggesting anno domini

definitions.text: His artful signature suggesting anno domini

blocks.note: surface reading: a sly forger, with a hint of the Artful Dodger across the grid

blocks.clueFragment: His artful signature suggesting anno domini
blocks.note: setter's reading: an artist who signed his work with a monogram of a large A over a small D

explanation.walkthrough: The German Renaissance artist Albrecht signed with his initials stacked as a monogram, which reads like AD, short for anno domini.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter and engraver's famous monogram formed from his two initials looks just like the date abbreviation.

clue.text: Riddle for star-gazers

definitions.note: the clue describes the thing star-gazers look at rather than naming them

blocks.note: first meaning: a coarse sieve for grading soil or gravel
second meaning: what film fans gaze at to watch the stars

explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' suggests a puzzle and 'star-gazers' astronomers; both are misdirection, toward a garden sieve and the cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: A screen is a large sieve, the same tool as a riddle, and also the surface where film actors appear.

clue.text: Supplementing a note with a sovereign?

blocks.note: E is one of the musical notes A to G
a sovereign is a reigning monarch

explanation.surface: Topping up a banknote with a gold sovereign coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' and 'sovereign' look like money, a banknote and an old gold coin; they are a musical note and a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out something is to make it last by adding to it, so the participle means supplementing.

clue.text: Victim of the firstborn

blocks.note: surface reading: a victim of the Egyptian plague that killed every firstborn
setter's reading: Cain, Adam and Eve's first son, who murdered his younger brother

explanation.walkthrough: The plague on Egypt's firstborn is the false trail; here the firstborn is the killer, not the victim.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the younger brother was murdered by Cain, the first child born to Adam and Eve.

clue.text: We get this day by day

definitions.text: We get this day by day

blocks.clueFragment: We get this day by day
blocks.note: surface reading: something delivered daily, like a newspaper or the post
setter's reading: every passing day adds to our age

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' sounds like receiving something, but it means become.
explanation.definitionFit: Each day that passes adds to a person's age, so we all become more aged daily.

clue.text: Dawkins J would make a crafty fly-half

blocks.note: first meaning: Jack Dawkins, the young pickpocket's real name in Dickens's Oliver Twist
second meaning: a cunning rugby half-back who sidesteps tacklers

explanation.walkthrough: The initial after the surname looks like a team sheet entry; a fly-half is the rugby back who runs and evades.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Dawkins is the Dickens character known by this nickname, and the phrase also literally means a cunning evader.
